connection: Session 9 covered ref/out/in. This session contrasts ClockEntry and Employee's default reference equality with WorkSummary's real record value equality (introduced in Session 22), and looks at where string comparison rules actually matter in this codebase.
objectives: Predict, and then confirm, that two separately-constructed ClockEntry objects with identical EmployeeId/ClockIn/ClockOut are NOT equal by default -- neither ClockEntry nor Employee overrides Equals.
Confirm that two WorkSummary records with the same EmployeeId and Hours ARE equal, because record types generate value-based equality automatically.
Explain why EmployeeDirectory's city-uniqueness check uses StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase rather than default string equality.
Distinguish struct value-copy semantics (WorkCode, a record struct) from class reference semantics (ClockEntry, Employee).

visuals.title: class gives you reference equality unless you opt out
visuals.explanation: new ClockEntry(1, t) != new ClockEntry(1, t) is true (they are unequal) -- ClockEntry never overrode Equals, so two separately-constructed objects are never equal, even with identical field values.

visuals.title: record gives you value equality automatically
visuals.explanation: new WorkSummary(1, 8m) == new WorkSummary(1, 8m) is true -- the compiler generates Equals/GetHashCode from WorkSummary's declared members.

visuals.title: Case sensitivity is a choice, not a default
visuals.explanation: "Springfield" == "springfield" is false under ordinal string comparison; EmployeeDirectory explicitly opts into StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase to treat them as the same city.

visuals.title: record struct copies by value, like int or DateTime
visuals.explanation: WorkCode is declared readonly record struct -- assigning one WorkCode variable to another copies its Year and Sequence, the same as any other value type.

options: No -- it uses the default reference equality inherited from object, so two ClockEntry objects with identical EmployeeId/ClockIn/ClockOut are still considered unequal
Yes -- it compares EmployeeId, ClockIn, and ClockOut
Yes, but only ClockOut is compared
preQuiz.explanation: Nothing in the real ClockEntry.cs overrides Equals or GetHashCode -- confirmed by reading the actual file; it relies entirely on object identity.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does new WorkSummary(1, 8m).Equals(new WorkSummary(1, 8m)) return true without any code written for it?
options: WorkSummary is declared as a record, and the compiler automatically generates member-wise Equals/GetHashCode/== for records
decimal always compares by value across all types
WorkSummary happens to be a singleton
preQuiz.explanation: record is a C# feature specifically for value-equality-by-default types -- WorkSummary gets this for free from its declaration, unlike the plain class ClockEntry.

preQuiz.prompt: What would "Springfield" == "springfield" evaluate to using C#'s default string equality?
options: false -- default string comparison is ordinal (case-sensitive) unless you explicitly choose a case-insensitive comparer
preQuiz.explanation: C#'s default == for string is ordinal and case-sensitive; EmployeeDirectory has to opt into StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase specifically to treat differently-cased city names as duplicates.

concept.title: ClockEntry and Employee: reference equality, by default and by choice
paragraphs: ClockEntry and Employee are both plain class declarations with no Equals override anywhere in the real source. That means == and .Equals() compare object identity: are these two variables pointing at the very same object?
This is a real, verified fact about the actual repository, not an assumption -- reading Models/ClockEntry.cs and Models/Employee.cs directly confirms neither type overrides equality members.

concept.title: WorkSummary: a record gets value equality automatically
paragraphs: public sealed record WorkSummary(int EmployeeId, decimal Hours) is a positional record. Declaring it with record instead of class is what generates member-wise Equals, GetHashCode, and == overloads -- no extra code required.
This is the real, meaningful contrast this session teaches: the same 'compare these two objects' question gets a different default answer depending on whether the type is declared class or record.

concept.title: String comparison is a choice you make explicitly
paragraphs: EmployeeDirectory's Cities set is constructed with new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) specifically so "Springfield" and "springfield" collapse into one entry.

Without that explicit comparer, HashSet<string>'s default ordinal comparison would treat them as two different cities -- exactly the kind of silent data-quality bug case-insensitive matching exists to prevent.
concept.code:
// src/TimeClock.Domain/EmployeeDirectory.cs
private readonly HashSet<string> cities = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

lab.objective: Confirm ClockEntry's reference equality and WorkSummary's record value equality with executable tests, and explain EmployeeDirectory's explicit string comparer choice.
lab.startingCondition: ClockEntry, WorkSummary, and EmployeeDirectory already exist with their real declarations.
steps: Write a test constructing two ClockEntry objects with identical arguments and assert they are NOT equal.
Write a test constructing two WorkSummary records with identical arguments and assert they ARE equal.
Temporarily remove StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase from EmployeeDirectory's cities field and observe a previously-passing uniqueness test start to fail.
Restore the comparer and confirm the test passes again.
lab.expectedBehavior: Two ClockEntry objects with equal field values are unequal by default; two equal-valued WorkSummary records are equal; removing OrdinalIgnoreCase breaks the case-insensitive city-uniqueness test.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntry were changed to a record instead of a class, what would change about existing code that stores ClockEntry objects in a List and looks them up by reference?
options: Value equality would mean two field-identical ClockEntry objects become interchangeable for Equals-based lookups, which could silently change behavior anywhere identity currently mattered (like GetClockEntry's FirstOrDefault)
Nothing would change -- record and class behave identically
The code would fail to compile
postQuiz.explanation: Switching class to record is not a purely cosmetic change -- it changes the equality semantics every consumer of that type relies on, which is exactly why this session treats it as a real design decision, not a syntax preference.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is WorkCode declared as a readonly record struct instead of a record (class)?
options: record struct combines record's generated value equality with struct's copy-by-value semantics -- appropriate for a small, immutable value like a year+sequence pair
record struct is required syntax for any type with two properties
There is no difference between record and record struct
postQuiz.explanation: record struct is specifically for small, copyable, value-equality types -- exactly what a WorkCode(Year, Sequence) pair is.

postQuiz.prompt: Would GetEmployeeClockEntries's real Where filter (entry.EmployeeId == employeeId) behave any differently if ClockEntry had record value equality instead of reference equality?
options: No -- that filter compares an int (EmployeeId) to an int, which already uses value equality regardless of whether ClockEntry itself is a class or record
Yes -- it would start matching by full object equality instead
postQuiz.explanation: The filter never compares whole ClockEntry objects to each other -- it compares one of their int fields, which is unaffected by ClockEntry's own equality semantics.

reflections: Why might a real codebase deliberately choose reference equality for ClockEntry rather than adding value equality?
What would you need to add to ClockEntry to make two field-identical instances equal, and what would you risk changing by doing so?
Where else in this codebase might case-insensitive string comparison matter, beyond EmployeeDirectory's city set?
whatBreaks: Assuming ClockEntry has value equality (because it superficially looks like a simple data holder) would lead to bugs anywhere code tries to deduplicate or compare ClockEntry objects by field value instead of by reference. Removing WorkSummary's record declaration in favor of class would silently break any test or code that currently relies on WorkSummary equality by value, including the real HoursByEmployee grouping test from Session 22. Removing EmployeeDirectory's StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase would let differently-cased city names silently multiply instead of being treated as one city.
summary: class gives you reference equality unless you explicitly override it -- confirmed true for both the real ClockEntry and Employee. record gives you value equality automatically, which is exactly why WorkSummary (Session 22's grouping result) compares equal across separately-constructed instances with the same values. String comparison is ordinal and case-sensitive by default; EmployeeDirectory's StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase is a deliberate, visible choice to treat city names case-insensitively.
